title: A Systematic Review of Optimization Algorithms for Structural Health Monitoring and Optimal Sensor Placement

subsections.subsection_title: Background and Evolution of Structural Health Monitoring
subsections.content:
Structural health monitoring (SHM) emerged from the convergence of classical non-destructive testing (NDT), experimental mechanics, and vibration-based system identification. Early monitoring practice was dominated by local inspections and strain measurements, reflecting a long instrumentation history in civil structures and the gradual maturation of sensing technologies over the first century of structural monitoring ref [3]. In parallel, broader NDT development established the conceptual basis for assessing integrity without interrupting service, spanning visual, ultrasonic, radiographic, acoustic, and electromagnetic methods that later became integral to SHM workflows ref [4].

A major shift occurred when researchers began treating global dynamic properties as damage indicators rather than relying solely on pointwise inspection. Seminal vibration-based studies showed that changes in stiffness alter modal characteristics and that natural-frequency measurements can be used not only to detect but also to localize damage from limited measurements ref [2], ref [10]. This transition was important because it reframed structures as continuously observable systems and motivated model-based inference, baseline comparison, and long-term condition tracking.

Subsequent evolution expanded SHM from metallic and civil components to heterogeneous and high-performance materials, especially composites, where embedded sensing, wave propagation, and multi-physics monitoring became increasingly important ref [1]. Modern SHM therefore represents a progression from periodic NDT toward persistent, data-rich, and often in-situ surveillance, with damage diagnosis now understood as a continuum from sensing and feature extraction to decision support and maintenance planning ref [1], ref [4].

subsections.subsection_title: Scope of Sensing and Damage Detection Technologies
subsections.content:
The sensing landscape in SHM is intrinsically multimodal, spanning contact and non-contact measurements of strain, vibration, temperature, displacement, acoustic response, and surface condition. Conventional electrical sensors, piezoelectric transducers, fiber-optic devices, electromagnetic probes, and camera-based systems each interrogate different damage-sensitive features and therefore support different detection tasks, from incipient crack sensing to global condition assessment ref [7], ref [8], ref [5]. In practice, the scope of sensing technology is best understood not by hardware alone, but by the physical observables it renders measurable under operational constraints.

Wave- and field-based methods remain central to damage detection. Piezoelectric transducers are widely used for guided-wave interrogation because of their compactness and actuation-sensing duality, while fiber Bragg grating sensors provide multiplexed strain and temperature measurements with strong immunity to electromagnetic interference; hybrid PZT/FBG configurations are especially attractive where complementary sensitivity and robustness are needed, as illustrated for railway-track damage detection using diffuse ultrasonic waves ref [8]. Electromagnetic sensing, including eddy-current approaches, is particularly effective for conductive components and becomes even more relevant in harsh or high-temperature environments, where recent reviews emphasize the importance of robust packaging, ceramic integration, and high-temperature-capable optical and inductive sensors ref [7].

A parallel expansion of SHM scope concerns vision-based and image-centric damage assessment. Image-based SHM now encompasses crack detection, displacement estimation, vibration tracking, corrosion mapping, and geometric change monitoring using digital cameras, UAV platforms, and computer-vision pipelines, often reducing installation burden relative to dense contact-sensor networks ref [5]. This breadth of sensing modalities motivates the central methodological question of the present survey: how to optimally select and place heterogeneous sensors so that complementary observables are captured with maximum information value under budget, accessibility, and environmental constraints.

subsections.subsection_title: Data-Driven SHM and Emerging Machine Learning Directions
subsections.content:
Recent SHM research has increasingly shifted from physics-guided but feature-engineered pipelines toward data-driven inference, where damage is identified directly from measured signals, images, or statistical representations. This transition is especially visible in vibration-based SHM, where conventional modal-feature workflows are being complemented by machine-learning and deep-learning models that better handle noise, environmental variability, and high-dimensional sensing data ref [9]. Experimental bridge studies also show the practical relevance of such approaches: data-based pipelines using autoregressive features and both supervised and unsupervised learning can detect multiple steel-bridge damage states with competitive performance even when labeled damaged data are limited, highlighting the value of anomaly detection and statistical learning for field deployment ref [10].

A major emerging direction is deep learning for automatic feature extraction. In contrast to earlier classifiers that rely on hand-crafted modal, spectral, or time-series descriptors, convolutional neural networks can learn hierarchical damage representations directly from raw or weakly processed inputs. In vision-based SHM, CNNs have achieved strong robustness for crack detection under challenging illumination, shadowing, blur, and scale variation, substantially outperforming traditional edge-based image processing in realistic concrete inspection scenarios ref [11]. Parallel developments in vibration-based SHM similarly exploit deep architectures to extract damage-sensitive features from mode shapes or response histories without explicit feature engineering, improving resilience to contaminated and incomplete data ref [9], ref [12].

These advances are expanding the methodological scope of SHM from pure detection toward scalable classification, localization, transfer learning, and cross-domain sensing fusion. At the same time, important challenges remain, including domain shift between laboratory and field data, scarcity of labeled damage cases, interpretability of learned features, and the need to integrate physical constraints with data-driven models. Accordingly, current survey trends point toward hybrid SHM frameworks that combine signal processing, statistical novelty detection, deep representation learning, and optimization-aware sensing strategies rather than treating them as isolated paradigms ref [9], ref [10], ref [12].

subsections.subsection_title: Sensor Placement and Optimization as a Methodological Theme
subsections.content:
Optimal sensor placement (OSP) is not merely an implementation detail in SHM, but a methodological bridge between structural modeling, sensing economics, and damage identifiability. Because practical deployments are constrained by cost, accessibility, bandwidth, and maintenance, OSP is typically posed as a combinatorial or discrete optimization problem over candidate degrees of freedom, with objectives linked to modal independence, information entropy, Fisher information, or damage sensitivity ref [5]. This framing makes sensor placement central to the reliability of downstream identification and diagnosis, rather than a separate hardware design stage ref [4], ref [5].

A key development in the OSP literature has been the move from heuristic ranking rules toward explicit optimization under discrete constraints. Sun and Buyukozturk formulate OSP as an integer optimization problem and show that modal-assurance-criterion-based objectives, coupled with penalty handling of placement constraints, can be effectively solved by discrete artificial bee colony search on reduced-order structural models ref [5]. Their case studies, including a truss bridge, an MIT high-rise building, and Canton Tower, illustrate a recurring lesson in SHM: the optimal layout depends strongly on both the structural model and the information criterion being optimized ref [5].

This dependence naturally links OSP to the broader optimization literature. Since objective evaluations may arise from finite-element simulations, modal truncation, or black-box performance metrics, derivative information is often unavailable or unreliable; hence derivative-free optimization provides an important conceptual and algorithmic foundation for SHM sensor layout design ref [15]. In practice, OSP studies have therefore adopted a wide spectrum of solvers, including genetic algorithms, particle swarm methods, monkey algorithms, Bayesian sequential schemes, and derivative-free direct-search variants, reflecting the mixed discrete, nonconvex, and computationally expensive nature of the problem ref [15], ref [5].

Large-scale landmark structures further demonstrate the practical maturity of this theme. For Canton Tower, optimized layouts based on modal criteria and metaheuristic search were shown to improve monitoring informativeness under realistic constraints, making OSP a prerequisite for scalable high-rise SHM rather than a post hoc refinement ref [4]. Accordingly, this survey treats optimization-based sensor placement as a unifying methodological theme: it connects sensing design with model reduction, uncertainty management, and damage-detection performance, and it remains one of the clearest points of convergence between classical SHM and contemporary computational intelligence ref [15], ref [4], ref [5].

subsections.section_title: Optimal Sensor Placement Methods and Criteria
subsections.subsection_title: Application-Specific Sensor Placement in Structural Health Monitoring
subsections.content:
Application-specific sensor placement in SHM is strongly shaped by the sensing modality, target structural behavior, and deployment constraints. In aerospace applications, early work on large space structures emphasized prelaunch selection of non-relocatable on-orbit sensors so that target modes remain linearly independent and suitable for model correlation, leading to effective-independence style ranking based on the Fisher information matrix ref [16]. For bridge monitoring, the objective is often broader: not only locating sensors, but also determining the minimum number of sensing nodes needed to recover vertical and torsional mode shapes with acceptable modal assurance, as demonstrated for both finite-element and field-data cases ref [17].

In civil infrastructure monitored by wireless sensor networks, placement must additionally account for communication energy, routing, and network survivability. Energy-aware deployment studies show an explicit trade-off between modal estimation quality and communication cost, motivating joint optimization of inter-node spacing and data-collection topology rather than purely modal criteria ref [18]. Similarly, fault-tolerant SHM deployment augments engineering-optimal primary locations with backup or relay-like sensing nodes to preserve connectivity and damage-detection capability under sensor or link failures ref [19]. These studies illustrate that, in practical WSN-based SHM, optimality is application-level rather than criterion-level alone ref [18], ref [19].

For guided-wave SHM, the placement problem changes again: actuator-sensor geometry relative to cracks, slots, and boundaries governs the clarity of reflected and transmitted wave packets. Numerical-experimental studies on Lamb-wave damage detection show that sensors placed near damage and along favorable propagation paths yield stronger damage-sensitive amplitude changes, whereas off-path or boundary-dominated locations can obscure interpretation ref [20]. Thus, application-specific placement in SHM is best viewed as a coupling between structural physics, sensing technology, and operational constraints, rather than a single universal optimization problem ref [16], ref [17], ref [20].

subsections.section_title: Optimal Sensor Placement Methods and Criteria
subsections.content:
Theoretical work on optimal sensor placement (OSP) in structural health monitoring is rooted in observability, identifiability, and information maximization. Early formulations cast OSP as selecting the minimum-cost sensor set that satisfies prescribed performance constraints, while later work clarified that the central issue is not mere observability, but the quality of state or parameter reconstruction under noise, redundancy, and modeling uncertainty ref [21], ref [25], ref [26]. In dynamic testing, this led to a progression from heuristic modal-amplitude rules toward rigorous criteria based on Fisher information, linear independence of target mode shapes, and reduced-estimation covariance ref [7], ref [25].

Accordingly, OSP evaluation criteria in SHM are commonly grouped into modal-independence and information-theoretic families. The effective independence/Fisher information perspective seeks sensor sets that maximize the determinant, trace, or conditioning of the information matrix, thereby improving parameter identifiability and reducing estimation uncertainty ref [26], ref [7]. Closely related criteria include modal assurance, residual covariance, observability, robustness to sensor loss, and damage-class separability ref [21], ref [25]. For high-density or mid-frequency regimes, frequency-response and principal-component formulations generalize modal criteria by using dominant response subspaces rather than a small set of modes ref [26].

Information entropy offers a complementary foundation, especially when damage detection is formulated as uncertainty reduction over candidate damage states. Entropy- and mutual-information-based criteria quantify the expected information gain of a sensor configuration, naturally balancing relevance against redundancy ref [22], ref [23], ref [25]. In practice, the choice of criterion should follow the SHM objective: modal testing favors identifiability and independence measures, whereas diagnosis and localization often benefit from entropy, class separability, and reliability-aware metrics ref [22], ref [25], ref [7].

subsections.section_title: Optimal Sensor Placement Methods and Criteria
subsections.subsection_title: Annealing, Tabu, and Other Metaheuristic Search Strategies
subsections.content:
Beyond evolutionary and swarm paradigms, simulated annealing (SA), tabu search (TS), and related metaheuristics remain attractive for optimal sensor placement (OSP) because they handle discrete, nonlinear, and multimodal search spaces without requiring gradients. Classical SA established the key idea of probabilistically accepting uphill moves to escape local minima, with solution quality strongly dependent on neighborhood design and cooling schedule ref [30]. In multiobjective settings, archived variants such as AMOSA extend this logic to Pareto search and are relevant when OSP must jointly balance identification accuracy, redundancy, and sensor cost ref [27].

Within structural health monitoring, annealing-based OSP has been used to optimize mode-shape observability and modal discrimination, with improved SA schemes reporting better placement robustness than straightforward modal heuristics ref [32]. Comparative studies further show that SA can outperform or complement genetic search depending on encoding, initialization, and convergence criteria, especially when the number of candidate locations is moderate and the objective landscape is rugged ref [7]. More broadly, surveys of simulated annealing and physics-inspired optimization emphasize that such methods are particularly effective when controlled diversification is needed and exact combinatorial formulations become prohibitive ref [29], ref [30].

Tabu search offers a different balance between intensification and diversification by using adaptive memory rather than temperature. In OSP for SHM and moving-force identification, TS has been implemented with modal assurance criterion (MAC)-based objectives and shown competitive or superior performance against EFI and ECEFI baselines under condition-number, Fisher-information, and reconstruction-error criteria ref [8]. Although these approaches are less common than evolutionary methods, they are valuable for application-specific OSP formulations where neighborhood structure, constraint handling, or multi-criterion trade-offs favor memory-based or annealing-style exploration ref [27], ref [32], ref [8].

subsections.section_title: Optimal Sensor Placement Methods and Criteria
subsections.subsection_title: Broader Optimization Context and Emerging Intelligent Methods
subsections.content:
Optimal sensor placement (OSP) in structural health monitoring should be understood within a broader optimization context: the suitability of any search strategy depends on the problem structure, constraints, and performance metric rather than on a universally superior optimizer. This perspective is consistent with the algorithm selection problem, which argues for matching algorithms to problem classes, and with no-free-lunch results showing that average superiority across all optimization problems is impossible ref [33], ref [5]. For SHM, this implies that sensor placement methods must be chosen with explicit regard to modal identifiability, damage sensitivity, sparsity, communication cost, and installation constraints rather than by optimizer popularity alone ref [5].

This broader view has encouraged movement beyond classical single-algorithm heuristics toward hybrid, data-informed, and learning-assisted OSP frameworks. In particular, surrogate-assisted optimization, multi-fidelity modeling, and automated algorithm configuration are attractive when repeated finite-element evaluations or uncertainty propagation make direct search expensive. Such developments align with the growing role of machine learning in SHM, where deep architectures provide powerful representation learning for damage diagnosis, multimodal fusion, and feature extraction from high-dimensional sensing streams ref [8]. Accordingly, sensor placement is increasingly coupled with downstream inference performance, not merely with geometric coverage or modal independence ref [8].

Emerging intelligent methods also point to a tighter integration between placement design and end-task analytics. Deep-learning-based SHM systems using multi-sensor fusion demonstrate that the value of a sensor layout depends on how effectively heterogeneous signals can be fused for diagnosis; optimized deep stacked autoencoders, for example, have shown strong potential for automated damage assessment in concrete structures ref [9]. This suggests a shift from purely physics- or information-criterion-based OSP toward co-optimization of sensing, feature learning, and decision quality. In practice, the most promising direction is therefore not a single new metaheuristic, but adaptive frameworks that combine domain knowledge, optimization theory, and intelligent data-driven models ref [33], ref [5], ref [8], ref [9].

subsections.section_title: Optimal Sensor Placement Methods and Criteria
subsections.subsection_title: Evolutionary and Swarm-Based Optimization for Sensor Placement
subsections.content:
Evolutionary and swarm-based methods have become a major branch of optimal sensor placement (OSP) in structural health monitoring because they handle the discrete, nonlinear, and often multimodal nature of sensor-layout search without requiring gradient information. In this literature, genetic algorithms (GAs) and particle swarm optimization (PSO) are especially prominent. Foundational PSO studies established the population-based update mechanism and clarified its effectiveness for both continuous and discrete optimization, including engineering design settings relevant to OSP ref [7], ref [8]. These features motivated direct adaptation to sensor placement, where candidate layouts can be naturally encoded as binary or integer strings and optimized against criteria such as modal assurance criterion (MAC), Fisher information matrix (FIM), and modal energy measures ref [37], ref [38], ref [39].

Among PSO-based OSP studies, Qin and Lin formulated the sensor-location problem as an integer program and showed that PSO can optimize layouts under MAC, FIM, or hybrid MAC–FIM criteria, highlighting the trade-off between modal linear independence and noise-robust parameter estimation ref [37]. GA-based variants similarly focused on representation and search operators. Fu and Yu combined MAC with a single-parenthood genetic algorithm (SPGA), using QR-based initialization and specialized gene exchange, shift, and inversion operations to improve convergence speed and reliability over conventional GA and sequential accumulation strategies ref [38]. For space structures, Beygzadeh et al. proposed an improved GA integrating a geometrical-viewpoint operator to bias mutation toward noise-resilient degrees of freedom, reporting faster convergence and more accurate damage detection than a standard GA under static and dynamic loading ref [39].

Recent work extends this line from single-objective optimization toward Pareto-based decision support. A decomposition-based multiobjective evolutionary framework coupled with discrete PSO was shown to jointly balance mode-shape independence, signal redundancy, and vibration response strength, yielding a Pareto set and then a closeness-based decision rule for final sensor selection ref [40]. This direction is important because no single criterion consistently dominates across SHM tasks. Overall, evolutionary and swarm methods are attractive not merely for global search capability, but for their flexibility in encoding application-specific criteria, hybridizing with deterministic preselection, and supporting multiobjective trade-off analysis in large candidate spaces ref [40], ref [7], ref [8].

Figures and tables should be used to synthesize the heterogeneity of optimization algorithms, sensing modalities, and application domains in SHM-oriented OSP studies. A preferred first figure is a PRISMA-style flowchart documenting search, screening, eligibility, and inclusion, as routinely adopted in systematic reviews of SHM, imaging-based monitoring, and composite-structure monitoring to improve transparency and reproducibility [1,2,3]. A complementary taxonomy figure can then classify the literature by optimizer family—evolutionary, swarm-based, annealing-based, tabu-search, discrete, and derivative-free—while linking each family to representative SHM formulations and sensor technologies [4,5,6,7,8,9].

Tables should carry the main comparative burden. One summary table should report, for each study, the structure type, objective function, optimization variables, constraints, number/type of sensors, and validation setting; this format is particularly useful because OSP formulations range from modal assurance and information-entropy criteria to frequency-based damage localization, Lamb-wave layouts, and wireless-network deployment objectives [10,11,12,13,14,15,16,17]. A second table can compare algorithmic behavior—single vs. multiobjective search, computational cost, convergence evidence, and robustness to combinatorial scaling—drawing on representative GA, SA, tabu, discrete, and decomposition-based approaches [18,19,20,21,22,23,24].

Result figures should emphasize trends rather than isolated case studies. Effective choices include heat maps of publication counts by optimizer and application, bar charts of structure classes (bridges, towers, space structures, railway tracks, high-temperature systems), and network diagrams connecting sensing technologies to target damage mechanisms [25,26,27,28,29]. Finally, a concise benchmark table is valuable for reporting whether studies provide experimental validation, numerical-only evidence, or field deployment, because this distinction remains central in SHM reviews and strongly affects the interpretability of claimed optimization gains [30,31,32].
